clue.text: Girl put on article the wrong way round

indicators.note: something put on the wrong way round faces backwards, so the article is read from its end

blocks.note: to don clothes is to put them on

explanation.surface: A girl has pulled on some item of clothing back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' sounds like a garment but is the grammar word.
explanation.definitionFit: Donna is an ordinary female first name, so it serves as an example of a girl.

clue.text: Is doing as badly — that's the doctor's opinion

indicators.note: something done badly is muddled, so the letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A doctor gives the verdict that a patient is in poor health.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagnosis is a physician's identification of an illness, a professional judgement.

clue.text: Frilly thing that is a garment worn in bed

indicators.note: frills are fussy ruffles, so the word is ruffled into another order

explanation.surface: A frilly item that is meant for wearing in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frilly' looks like a description of the nightwear itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightie is an informal word for a nightdress, worn for sleeping.

clue.text: Fruit in a container mostly loaded inside

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
inside places one piece within the other

explanation.surface: Fruit is packed into a container, nearly full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' suggests a filled container; it is the slang for rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The apricot is an orange stone fruit, so it is an example of fruit.

clue.text: Pole eggs on employer at a dance

blocks.note: the boss is the one who employs you
ova is the Latin plural for eggs

explanation.surface: A Polish worker pelts the boss with eggs at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the pole-plus-eggs piece after the employer and the 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bossa nova is a Brazilian style of music and the dance performed to it.

clue.text: Cocktail made by brother Andrew and another boy

explanation.surface: Two lads, one of them a brother called Andrew, mix a cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy alexander is a mixed drink of brandy, crème de cacao and cream.

clue.text: Buy drinks with drop of gin in, then refuse to move

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the first letter is taken
in places this letter within the drinks phrase

blocks.note: to pay for a round of drinks for the group

explanation.surface: Someone buys a round with gin in it, then won't leave the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, standing your round means paying for the next set of drinks for your group in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand one's ground is to hold firm and not retreat, an idiom for refusing to move.

clue.text: Region containing a lake, salt lake

indicators.note: containing means holding the next pieces inside

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: An area that holds a saline body of water.
explanation.walkthrough: The area must hold A, L and S; only the first letter of 'salt' fits, which leaves 'lake' as the definition, though 'salt lake' reads as one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aral Sea, despite its name, is a large saline lake in Central Asia.

clue.text: Ring girl about trendy wind instrument

indicators.note: about means going round, so the girl surrounds the next piece

blocks.note: a ring has the shape of the letter

explanation.surface: Someone phones a girlfriend about a fashionable woodwind instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call; it is the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocarina is a small egg-shaped flute, blown like a whistle.

clue.text: Former US president produces a manuscript after a bit of delay

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its first letter
after means this piece comes later in the answer than the next one

explanation.surface: A one-time American president hands in a manuscript late.
explanation.definitionFit: John Adams and his son John Quincy Adams were both presidents of the United States.

clue.text: Unusually large one, a republic in Africa

indicators.note: something done unusually is done out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An unusually big example of an African republic is being described.
explanation.definitionFit: Algeria is a North African country that has been a republic since independence from France.

clue.text: Either way, it's a popular novel

definitions.text: Either way, it's a popular novel

blocks.clueFragment: Either way, it's a popular novel
blocks.note: surface reading: whatever you think of it, this book sells well
setter's reading: the title of this genre of novel reads the same forwards and backwards

explanation.surface: A bestselling book that works just as well whichever direction you take it.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a big range cooker found in well-off country kitchens; an Aga saga is a light novel about middle-class rural family life. The answer happens to be a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Aga sagas are commercially popular fiction, so the phrase names a type of popular novel.

clue.text: Saw how most teas are served?

blocks.note: second meaning, split in two words: not chilled, i.e. served hot

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, NOT ICED, for the second meaning; the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to see it, so the past tense matches saw.

clue.text: Cashier one Sergeant Major in Norfolk town

indicators.note: to be in a town is to be placed within it

blocks.note: Diss is a market town in Norfolk, an English county

explanation.surface: A sergeant major in a small Norfolk town is working as a cashier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cashier' looks like a noun for a till worker, but here it is the verb. The inserted pair goes in as sergeant major then one.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to discharge them from the service, so it means to sack or send away.

clue.text: Charming girl's let in boy for nothing

blocks.note: sweet can mean charming or endearing
the possessive ending supplies its letter

explanation.surface: A charming young woman has allowed a boy in without charging anything.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on 'girl' gives the final letter after the boy's name. Sweet Fanny Adams, or 'sweet FA', is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang phrase means nothing at all, absolutely zero.

clue.text: Parting and sides showing signs of poor hair

blocks.note: a split is a parting or separation
the ends of something are its sides or extremes

explanation.surface: A hairdresser notes a parting and the sides of a head of unhealthy hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parting' looks like a line in the hair, but it is a separation.
explanation.definitionFit: Split ends are frayed hair tips, a symptom of dry or damaged hair.

clue.text: Dog nearing slippers goes wild

indicators.note: something that goes wild runs out of control, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A dog getting close to its owner's slippers becomes very excited.
explanation.definitionFit: The springer spaniel is a breed of gun dog, so it is an example of a dog.

clue.text: Novelist aboard called nervously on the way up

indicators.note: aboard means carried within, so the name sits inside the words given
in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A writer on board a plane is called and goes up nervously.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth Rendell was an English crime novelist, so she is an example of a novelist.

clue.text: Crank, one with an obsessive interest over lawsuit

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: an enthusiast, as in a fitness nut

explanation.surface: An eccentric with an obsession is pursuing a lawsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crank' looks like a verb or a handle; it is a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A crank is an eccentric person, and a nutcase is an informal word for someone mad.

clue.text: Assign a parking place

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
a point is a location or place

explanation.surface: An attendant allocates a parking space.
explanation.definitionFit: To appoint is to nominate someone to a role, which is to assign it to them.

clue.text: Settle a problem in golf club over Open

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above, so the club comes first

blocks.note: out can mean open, not hidden

explanation.surface: A dispute at a golf club about the Open championship is resolved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open' suggests the golf championship but means public, out in the open.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron out difficulties is an idiom for resolving them, smoothing creases away.

clue.text: Singer posed to accommodate popular artist

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to take them in and house them

blocks.note: an artist's model sat, or posed, for a portrait

explanation.surface: A singer sat for a portrait painted by a well-known artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Sinatra was the famous American crooner, so he is an example of a singer.

clue.text: American drink — Carol has litre brought in

indicators.note: to have something brought in is to hold it inside

explanation.surface: Carol, a woman, orders a litre of an American drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A sling is a mixed drink of spirit, sugar and water, originally American.

clue.text: Music and drink brings affinity

explanation.surface: Good tunes and a few drinks help people get along.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapport is a close, harmonious relationship, so it matches affinity as a synonym.

clue.text: One about to put down British composer

blocks.note: to land a plane is to put it down

explanation.surface: Someone is on the point of putting a British composer down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' suggests criticism, but it is landing an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: John Ireland was an English composer of the early twentieth century, so he is an example.

clue.text: A French counterfeit coin bearing head of really fabulous beast

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter
a counterfeit is a fake, so the letters are made up into something false

explanation.surface: A fake French coin is stamped with the image of a mythical creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes the coin's letters plus the first letter of 'really'.
explanation.definitionFit: A unicorn is a mythical horse with one horn, so fabulous here means legendary.

clue.text: Information given by staff about mature garden plant

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the information goes round the other piece

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
old means grown up or aged
a rod is a stick or staff

explanation.surface: A member of staff hands out advice about a mature plant in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' suggests employees, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldenrod is a perennial with yellow flower spikes, commonly grown in borders.

clue.text: Emperor from Chianti, Tuscany

indicators.note: from means the answer is taken out of the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of the wine's name plus the start of the region

explanation.surface: A Roman emperor with a taste for wine from Tuscany.
explanation.definitionFit: Titus was a Roman emperor of the Flavian dynasty, so he is an example.
